I dedicate this book to all the resilient mothers who strive to balance their careers and ongoing professional growth amidst the chaos of daily life and family responsibilities. I would also like to acknowledge my wonderful husband, whose unwavering support and encouragement lifted my spirits during my lowest moments. It is thanks to his steadfast assistance that I have been able to accomplish this significant endeavor. I am deeply grateful to my parents and my cherished children, whose joyful smiles inspire me and provide the motivation to keep pushing forward.
I declare that this book is my original work and has not
been published elsewhere. All sources have been duly
acknowledged. There is no conflict of interest.

This book is a humble effort born from a desire to see my peers excel. As I share this work with you, I also share a piece of my own journey—one defined by persistence, sacrifice, and the pursuit of excellence. As a mother of three wonderful children, balancing the demands of family life with the rigors of medical specialization was a formidable challenge. However, I never lost hope. I kept pushing forward until I reached the point where I could finally compile my experiences and knowledge into this volume.

After graduating and earning the prestigious FCPS degree, I felt that a new pinnacle of achievement was still waiting for me. This led me to embark on the journey toward the MRCOG. During my preparation, I realized that the available study material was often haphazard, fragmented, and lacked a cohesive structure. Lengthy topics remained unsummarized, and many resources failed to integrate the latest guidelines and recommendations.

I recognized the urgent need for a single, concise resource—one that eliminates the need to juggle multiple files while ensuring no critical point is missed. Maternal mind is designed to be that ideal companion. By utilizing specialized flowsheets, I have distilled complex, lengthy topics into single-page summaries, making them easier to memorize and, more importantly, easier to reproduce under exam conditions.

In the end, I want to thank you for choosing this book. It is my sincere hope that this labor of love serves as a clear guide through your own professional journey, helping you reach your goals with confidence and clarity.

Perfect use: of a contraceptive method is when it is used correctly all the time.
Typical use: is what generally happens in real life. It takes into account human error.

content_blocks.content: This guideline will consider POPs available in the UK. namely Desogestrel (DSG) 75 kg, Drosperinone (DRSP) 4 mg (soon to be available in the UK) and the ‘traditional’ POPs levonorgestrel| (LNG) 30 pg and norethisterone (NET) 350 ug
MOA: DSG and DRSP POPs: inhibition of ovulation
LNG and NET POPs: changes on cervical mucus, endometrium and tubal motility
A 12-month supply of traditional, DSG or DRSP POP can be provided with an annual review.
Specific approved brands of DSG POP can now be bought from a pharmacy, without a prescription, under the supervision of a pharmacist.
LNG, NET and DSG POPs are taken continuously at 24-hour intervals without an HFI.
The new DRSP POP is taken in a regimen of 24 daily active pills followed by four hormone-free placebo pills (to establish a more predictable bleeding pattern)
Use of all POPs taken between menarche and age 55 years.
DRSP POP should also generally be avoided in:
Severe renal insufficiency or acute renal failure.
Individuals with known hyperkaliemia or untreated hyperaldosteronism (e.g., Addison's disease).
Individuals currently using potassium-sparing diuretics, aldosterone antagonists or potassium supplements.
DRSP POP used with caution by individuals with mild/moderate renal impairment or treated hyperaldosteronism (e.g., treated Addison's disease)

Individuals with significant risk factors for chronic kidney disease: measurement of urea & electrolytes (U&E) and blood pressure considered prior to prescription of the DRSP POP, particularly if age over 50 years
Side effects: Change in bleeding pattern over a 3-month period ending at about 12 months of use (at around 6—9 months of use with DRSP POP)
Interactions: contraceptive effectiveness of all POPs could be reduced during use of the enzyme-inducer and for 28 days after stopping the enzyme-inducer.
Ability of UPA-EC as an EC can be reduced if a POP has been taken in the preceding 7 days or within 5 days of taking the UPA. Offer them DMPA. the Cu-lUD or the LNG-IUS
Interactions between DRSP POP and drugs such as ACEi and ARBs could also potentially increase risk of hyperkaliemia
DSG and DRSP POP could reduce dysmenorrhea for some users
DRSP POP might theoretically offer benefit for acne or hirsutism
Induction of withdrawal bleeding is not required in individuals with PCOS during use of a POP even if they are amenorrhea.
AC: additional contraception like barrier or abstinence

DRSP POP is started on day 1 of a natural menstrual cycle, day 1 after abortion or by day 21 after childbirth. If started at any other time, quick start+ AC for 7 days+ consider EC and follow-up pregnancy test

LNG, NET and DSG POPs can be started on days 1—5 of a natural menstrual cycle, by day 5 after abortion or by day 21 after childbirth. At any other time. quick start +AC for 2 days+ consider EC and follow-up pregnancy test if required.
(UPSI from the time that the first pill was missed until correct pill taking had resumed for 48 hours)

POPs increase volume & viscosity of cervical mucus preventing sperm penetration into upper reproductive tract. Can also act to suppress ovulation.
If used consistently and correctly, POPs are more than 99% effective.
POP users taking enzyme-inducing drugs should be advised to switch to the progestogen-only injectable or intrauterine contraception.
For short durations of enzyme-inducing treatment (<2 months) women can continue the POP providing they use additional precautions
Women wishing to start the POP after stopping enzyme-inducing drugs should be advised dafter the last dose of enzyme-inducing drug.
(>27 hours since the last pill was taken) (>36 hours since the last pill was taken)
The missed pill should be taken as soon as remembered. If more than one pill has been missed, only one pill should be taken.
The next pill should be taken at the usual time. This may mean that two pills are taken in 1 day.
Additional contraceptive precautions (condoms or avoidance of sex) are advised for 2 days (48 hours) after restarting the POP.
Emergency contraception is indicated if unprotected sexual intercourse occurred after the missed pill and within 48 hours of restarting the POP.
NO increased risk of pregnancy in POP users with a heavier body weight or a higher BMI and insufficient evidence to support a dose of more than one pill per day in women who are heavy or overweight.
Ectopic pregnancy: While the overall risk of pregnancy is reduced with use of traditional POPs, around 1 in 10 pregnancies that do occur may be ectopic.
Headaches and Ovarian cysts/persistent ovarian follicles: No good evidence was identified.

Return of fertility: There is no evidence suggesting a delay in return of fertility following discontinuation of a POP; therefore, if pregnancy is not desired, other contraceptive methods should be used immediately following discontinuation of the POP.
Bleeding: Changes in bleeding patterns associated with the POP are common.
Libido: Effects of POP on libido are lacking and therefore a possible effect cannot be excluded.
Weight change: Evidence does not support a casual association between POP use and weight change.
Women may be given up to a 12-month supply of POPs at their first and follow-up visits and advised to return at any time if problems arise.
The POP can be used until the age of 55 years when natural loss of fertility can be assumed for most women.
If they are aged > 50 years and amenorrhea they can continue using a POP and have FSH concentrations tested on two occasions 6 weeks apart. If both FSH measurements are >30 IU/I this is

topics.title: 11. PROGESTOGEN-ONLY INJECTABLE CONTRACEPTION
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 11. PROGESTOGEN-ONLY INJECTABLE CONTRACEPTION.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: ▪ Long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs) are those that are administered less frequently than once a month.
DMPA (Depot Medroxyprogesterone Acetate) and NET-EN (Norethisterone Enanthate) are long-acting progestogens.
Depo-Provera: 150 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate in 1 ml.
Also available as a subcutaneous (SC) injection:
Sayana Press: 104 mg MPA in 0.65 ml
Less commonly used in the UK.
Given as Noristerat®: 200 mg in 1 ml via IM injection.
Licensed for short-term use, such as:
When a partner has undergone vasectomy (until successful vasectomy is confirmed).
The combined contraceptive injectable is not available in the UK.

Mode of action: Progestogen-only injectable contraception works primarily by inhibiting ovulation. There is also an effect on cervical mucus, resulting in poor cervical mucus scores and limited sperm penetration.
Failure rate: When administered at the recommended dosing interval the failure rate of progestogen-only injectable contraception is approximately 0.2% in the first year of use.
With typical use the failure rate is approximately 6%.

Bleeding and dysmenorrhea:Amenorrhea or reduced bleeding is common in progestogen-only injectable users and may benefit women with menstrual problems. DMPA use may reduce pain associated with endometriosis. Women should be advised about changes in bleeding patterns.
Ovarian and endometrial cancers:Use of DMPA is not associated with an increased risk of ovarian or endometrial cancer and may offer some protection.
Sickle cell disease:DMPA is a contraceptive option for women with sickle cell disease and may reduce the severity of sickle crisis pain.
Bone mineral density (BMD):Progestogen-only injectable use is associated with a small loss of BMD, which is usually recovered after discontinuation.
In women aged under 18 years, progestogen-only injectable contraception can be used after consideration of alternative methods.
Women are generally advised to switch to another method at age 50 years.
No DMPA before 18years and after 50 years
Breast cancer: There is a weak association between current use of DMPA and breast cancer. Any increased risk is likely to be small and reduce with time after stopping
Cardiovascular health: A causal association between DMPA and venous thrombosis has not been demonstrated.

Cervical cancer: There is a weak association between cervical cancer and use of DMPA for 5 years or longer. Any increased risk appears to reduce with time after stopping and could be due to confounding factors.
Altered bleeding patterns and Weight gain: Use of DMPA appears to be associated with weight gain, particularly in women under 18 years of age with a BMI >30kg/m2.
Injection site reactions: Injection site reactions appear to be more common with use of SC DMPA than with use of IM DMPA.
Others Effects: Diffuse hair loss (alopecia), Headache, Mood change, Vasomotor symptoms,   Libido and sexual function,

Vaginitis: Whilst there is little evidence available to demonstrate causation, a number of possible side effects such as acne, decreased libido, mood swings, headache, hot flushes and vaginitis have been reported with use of DMPA.
The gluteal muscle is the preferred site for IM DMPA administration but it can be administered into the deltoid muscle of SC DMPA should be injected into the abdomen or anterior thigh.

Women should be advised to return fora repeat injection of IM or SC DMPA (outside the product license for IM DMPA). An injection of DMPA can be administered up to 7 days late (up to 14 weeks after the last injection) without the need for additional contraceptive
precautions (outside the product license for IM DMPA).
The efficacy of DMPA is not reduced with concurrent use of enzyme-inducing drugs.
No increased risk of pregnancy has been demonstrated in progestogen-only injectable users with higher body weight, although data are limited in women with a BMI >40 kg/m².

Return of fertility:Women who discontinue their progestogen-only injectable and who do not wish to conceive should be advised to start another contraceptive method before or at the time of their next scheduled injection even if amenorrhoeic.
Women should be informed that there can be a delay of up to 1 year in the return of fertility after discontinuation of IM or SC DMPA.

Sexually transmitted infections and testing:The consistent and correct use of condoms (male or female) can reduce the risk of STI transmission and should therefore be recommended as a risk-reduction strategy.
Women who experience unscheduled bleeding during use of a progestogen-only injectable and who are medically eligible can be offered a COC for 3 months.
Women with unscheduled bleeding during use of a progestogen-only injectable contraceptive can be offered 500 mg mefenamic acid up to three times daily for 5 days.

topics.title: 12. PROGESTOGEN-ONLY IMPLANT
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 12. PROGESTOGEN-ONLY IMPLANT.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: The ENG-IMP is currently the only progestogen-only contraceptive subdermal implant available in the UK.
The ENG-IMP is a highly effective long-acting reversible method of contraception.
Licensed for 3 years of use for contraception.
The first-year contraceptive failure rate for the ENG-IMP has been estimated at 0.05%.
Routine use of the ENG-IMP for longer than 3 years is not currently recommended.

Women using enzyme-inducing drugs should be informed that the contraceptive effectiveness of the ENG-IMP could be reduced during use of the enzyme-inducer and for 28 days after stopping the enzyme-inducer.
Women using enzyme-inducing drugs should be offered a reliable contraceptive method that is unaffected by enzyme-inducers.
The available evidence suggests that contraceptive effectiveness of ENG is not affected by body weight or BMI
The ability of UPA-EC to delay ovulation could be reduced if an ENG-IMP is inserted within 5 days of taking the UPA.
The ability of UPA-EC to delay ovulation could theoretically be reduced if a woman has an ENG-IMP in situ (even if it has been in situ for longer than 3 years).
Individuals should be advised to wait 5 days after taking UPA-EC before insertion of the ENG-IMP.
They should be made aware that they must use condoms reliably or abstain from sex during the 5 days waiting and then for 7 days after implant insertion.
Breast cancer, arterial thromboembolism, decompensated cirrhosis, hepatocellular tumors and unexplained vaginal bleeding are UKMEC 3 or 4

Endometriosis: Limited available evidence suggests that use of the ENG-IMP could be associated with improvement in endometriosis- associated pain
Endometrial protection in polycystic ovary syndrome: Induction of withdrawal bleeding is not required in ENG-IMP users with polycystic
ovary syndrome who are amenorrhoeic during the licensed duration of use of the ENG-IMP
Venous and arterial thromboembolism:Evidence suggests no significant increase in risk of venous or arterial thromboembolic events associated with current use of the ENG-IMP.
Osteoporosis:Evidence is too limited to confirm or exclude an association between ENG-IMP use and reduction in bone mineral density (BMD).
Breast cancer:No significant increase in risk of breast cancer associated with ENG-IMP use but is too limited to completely exclude an association.
Gynecological cancer:The available evidence is too limited to inform whether an association exists between use of the ENG-IMP and risk of ovarian, endometrial, or cervical cancer.
Ectopic pregnancy:Risk of ectopic pregnancy during use of the ENG-IMP is extremely small.
Irregular, unpredictable bleeding is common during use of the ENG-IMP.
Bleeding pattern may change at any time during use of an ENG-IMP.
Individuals with ‘unfavorable’ bleeding patterns in the first few months after ENG-IMP insertion may have about a 50% chance that bleeding will improve over time.

Endometrial protection in polycystic ovary syndrome:Induction of withdrawal bleeding is not required in ENG-IMP users with polycystic ovary syndrome who are amenorrhoeic during licensed duration of use of ENG-IMP.
Note:After exclusion of other causes of bleeding, ENG-IMP users with problematic bleeding who are medically eligible can be offered a 3-
month trial of additional use of COC or a 5-day course of mefenamic acid.
Headache: Headache is commonly reported during ENG-IMP use; but limited evidence.
Acne: Observational studies suggest that during ENG-IMP use a minority of users experience new onset acne or worsening of existing acne while others have improvement in existing acne.
Depression: The available evidence is too limited to confirm or exclude a causative association between ENG-IMP use and depression.
Weight change: The available evidence is too limited to confirm or exclude a causal association between ENG-IMP use and weight gain.
Other side effects: Mastalgia (10.2% of women), abdominal pain (5.2%), dizziness (4.9%), emotional lability (5.7%), nervousness (3.5%) and nausea (2.5%).
Venous and arterial thromboembolism: evidence suggests no significant increase in risk of venous or arterial thromboembolic events associated with current use of the ENG-IMP.
Osteoporosis: evidence is too limited to confirm or exclude an association between ENG-IMP use and reduction in BMD.
Breast cancer: no significant increase in risk of breast cancer associated with ENG-IMP use but is too limited to completely exclude an association.
Gynecological cancer: The available evidence is too limited to inform whether an association between use of the ENG-IMP and risk of ovarian, endometrial or cervical cancer.
Ectopic pregnancy: risk of ectopic pregnancy during use of the ENG-IMP is extremely small.

Endometrial protection in polycystic ovary syndrome:Induction of withdrawal bleeding is not required in ENG-IMP users with polycystic ovary syndrome who are amenorrhoeic during licensed duration of use of ENG-IMP.

Note:After exclusion of other causes of bleeding, ENG-IMP users with problematic bleeding who are medically eligible can be offered a 3-month trial of additional use of COC or a 5-day course of mefenamic acid.

At any other time, the ENG-IMP can be quick started according to Quick Starting Guidance, with advice to use additional contraceptive precautions for 7 days and to take a follow-up pregnancy test (if required).

topics.title: 13. EMERGENCY CONTRACEPTION
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 13. EMERGENCY CONTRACEPTION.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: Indication: Women who do not wish to conceive should be offered EC after UPSI that has taken place on any day of a natural menstrual cycle.
After pregnancy: Women who do not wish to conceive should be offered EC after:
UPSI from Day 5 after abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or uterine evacuation for gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD).
Hormonal contraception incorrectly: Women who do not wish to conceive should be offered EC after UPSI if their regular contraception has been compromised or has been used incorrectly
Sperm are viable in the female genital tract for about 5 days after UPSI. If ovulation occurs within those 5 days, fertilization could take place and a woman is at risk of pregnancy.

Cu-lUD: Inhibition of fertilization by its toxic effect on sperm and ova. Copper has been shown to adversely affect the motility and viability of sperm and the viability and transport of ova. It is the most effective method of EC
UPA: UPA 30 mg – a selective progesterone receptor modulator – acts by delaying ovulation for at least 5 days, until sperm from the UPSI for which EC was taken are no longer viable.
LNG: LNG-EC inhibits ovulation, delaying or preventing follicular rupture and causing luteal dysfunction.
EC providers should advise women that UPA-EC has been demonstrated to be effective for EC up to 120 hours of UPSI
LNG-EC is licensed for EC up to 72 hours after UPSI. The evidence suggests that LNG-EC is ineffective if taken more than 96 hours after UPSI.

content_blocks.content: Male condoms (latex, non-latex, and deproteinized latex varieties)
Condoms (male and/or female): Men and women requesting condoms should be informed of the efficacy of condoms including their failure rate relative to other methods.

Diaphragms and caps: A diaphragm or cervical cap can be inserted with spermicide any time before intercourse. Spermicide should be reapplied if sex is to take place and the diaphragm or cap has been in situ for >3 hours or if sex is repeated with the method in place. A diaphragm or cervical cap should not be removed until at least 6 hours after the last episode of intercourse.
Barrier Methods at Preventing Transmission of STIs and other infections

Condoms recommendedSexually active men and women can be informed that the consistent and correct use of condoms (including with sex toys) is the most efficient means of protecting against HIV and other STIs.
Factors Affecting the Efficacy of Barrier Methods
Spermicides:Women using a diaphragm or cap should be advised to use the device with spermicide. The use of condoms lubricated with N-9 is not recommended.
Lubricants:When using lubricant with latex condoms, diaphragms, and caps, a water- or silicone-based preparation is recommended.
Size and shape:Ill-fitting condoms can be associated with breakage and incomplete use.

Legal issues:Health professionals should keep up to date with the important legal issues regarding HIV/STI transmission and advise patients appropriately as regards partner notification, disclosure and condom use.
Emergency contraception (EC) may be indicated in the following situations:
Diaphragm or cap is dislodged or removed within 6 hours of sex
Diaphragm has been left in for longer than 3 hours before sex and no additional spermicide applied
Failure to use condoms as advised when starting or switching contraception
If enzyme-inducing drugs are being used alongside hormonal contraception (combined hormonal contraception, POP and implant) and condoms are not used during or for 28 days after

Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV:Men and women can be made aware of PEPSE.For women living with HIV or at high risk of HIV infection, the use of either a diaphragm or cervical cap is a UKMEC Category 3.

The use of the diaphragm, cervical cap or contraceptive sponge is a UKMEC Category 3.
Women with a history of TSS may use male or female condoms.
Caps and diaphragms should not be left in situ for longer than recommended by the manufacturer or used during menstruation.

topics.title: 17. INTRAUTERINE CONTRACEPTION
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 17. INTRAUTERINE CONTRACEPTION.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: IUC methods are long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARC) with licensed durations of use ranging between 3 and 10 years.
The LNG-IUS is a T-shaped device with an elastomers core containing levonorgestrel (LNG).
The 52 mg LNG-IUS (Mirena) releases approximately 20 µg LNG per day, reducing to approximately 10 µg per day after 5 years.
The 13.5 mg LNG-IUS (Jaydess) is licensed for contraception and has a release rate of approximately 14 µg per day for the first 24 days, decreasing to 5 µg per day after 3 years.
Both pre- and post-fertilization effects, interfere with implantation, reduced rates of blastocyst formation.
Cu-IUD is effective immediately following insertion. If fertilization has already occurred, the endometrial inflammatory reaction has been shown to have an anti-implantation effect.

Contraceptive Efficacy and Duration of Use: Women advised of the very low failure rates.The most effective methods of IUC are the LNG-IUS methods and T-shaped devices with at least 380 mm² copper and copper bands on the transverse arms.
Criteria for excluding pregnancy She has not had intercourse since last normal menses
She has been correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception
She is within the first 7 days of the onset of a normal menstrual period
She is not breastfeeding and less than 4 weeks from giving birth
She is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months’ postpartum
She is within the first 7 days post-abortion or miscarriage
A negative pregnancy test, if available, adds weight to the exclusion of pregnancy, but only if ≥3 weeks since the last episode of unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI).
NB: In addition to the conditions mentioned above, health professionals should also consider whether a woman is at risk of becoming pregnant as a result of UPSI within the last 7 days.
Clinical assessment: detail history, UKMEC assessment before insertion.
STI risk assessment: A sexual history must be taken in order to identify women at risk of STI. Risk factors include:
Being sexually active and aged <25 years
Having a new sexual partner in the last 3 months
Having more than one sexual partner in the last year
Having a regular sexual partner who has other sexual partners
A history of STI and Alcohol/substance abuse
Attending as a previous contact of STI
Prophylactic antibiotics are not routinely required for the insertion or removal of IUC, even in women with conditions where the risk of infective endocarditis may be increased.
Dysmenorrhea/pelvic pain: primary dysmenorrhea, endometriosis or adenomyosis
Heavy menstrual bleeding: The 52 mg LNG-IUS is effective in reducing menstrual blood loss and can be used in the management of HMB.
Weight: Weight gain has been observed with use of IUC. There is no significant difference between hormonal & non-hormonal intrauterine methods and evidence to support a causal association is lacking.
Irregular Bleeding: In the 3–6 months following IUC insertion, women may experience irregular, prolonged or frequent bleeding, but menstrual bleeding patterns tend to improve with time.
Breast cancer: Evidence does not support a link between breast cancer and use of LNG-IUS. Non-hormonal contraception is most appropriate for women with a history of breast cancer.
Cardiovascular health: Evidence suggests there is little or no increased risk of VTE or MI associated with the use of a LNG-IUS.
Ectopic pregnancy: If pregnancy does occur with an intrauterine method in situ, the risk of an ectopic pregnancy occurring is increased.
The risk of expulsion with IUC is around 1 in 20 and is most common in the first year of use, particularly within 3 months of insertion.
There is no need to delay insertion of an IUC post-abortion providing woman has been informed of the small increased risk of expulsion.
Although ovarian cysts may occur when using the LNG-IUS, most cysts are asymptomatic and resolve spontaneously.
Cu-IUD users with recurrent BV or VVC may wish to consider an alternative method of contraception.
Valid consent should be given by women prior to both pelvic examination and IUC insertion or removal.
When inserting IUC, regardless of the setting, remember the following points:
Establish whether a reliable method of contraception was used before insertion and whether pregnancy can be excluded (see Box 1).
Obtain consent (written or verbal), including a description of the insertion procedure and the risks associated with it (failure rate, infection, expulsion and perforation).
Keep written documentation, including findings of bimanual and speculum examination.
Provide post-insertion information, including what to expect in terms of pain and bleeding and which symptoms should prompt urgent medical advice.
There is no evidence from current trials to support the use of topical lidocaine, misoprostol or NSAIDs for improving ease of insertion or reducing pain during insertion of intrauterine methods.
NSAIDs can be offered to women who experience pain after insertion of an intrauterine method. A bimanual pelvic examination should be performed on all women before inserting IUD.

✅ Unscheduled bleeding: For women with unscheduled bleeding who wish to continue with the LNG-IUS and are medically eligible,a COC could be tried for up to 3 months.NSAIDs can be considered in the management of problematic bleeding with use of Cu-IUDs.

Presence of actinomyces-like organisms (ALO):Insertion or reinsertion of an intrauterine method can be carried out in asymptomatic women with ALOs.There is no need to remove IUC in asymptomatic women with ALOs.
Suspected pelvic infection: IUD removal is not routinely required in women with PID but it should be removed if there is no response to treatment (approximately 72 hours)

Symptoms requiring medical attention: Women should be advised to seek medical assistance at any time if they develop symptoms of pelvic infection, pain, abnormal bleeding, late menstrual period (IUD), non-palpable threads or can feel the stem of the IUC.
Routine follow-up: A routine follow-up visit can be advised after the first menses following insertion of IUC or 3-6 weeks later.

For women with cardiac disease the decision to use IUD should involve a cardiologist. The IUD should be fitted in a hospital setting if a vasovagal reaction presents a particularly high risk, for example, women with single ventricle circulation, Eisenmenger physiology, tachycardia or pre-existing bradycardia.
Step 2: If not pregnant, advise alternative contraception and arrange ultrasound scan to locate the device
Step 3: If device located in uterus, assess for:
Leave in situ until due for removal, OR
Attempt removal with appropriate tools, OR
Request X-ray of abdomen and pelvis.
If device located on X-ray, assess for perforation and manage accordingly.
Key Guidelines for Timing of IUD Removal/Replacement:
Over 50 years of age: Remove 1 year after last menstrual period.
Under 50 years of age: Remove 2 years after last menstrual period.
If inserted at age 45 or above, it can be used for 7 years (instead of replacing at standard 5 years).
For planned pregnancy: Remove after pregnancy advice and lifestyle counseling.
When removed within licensed duration to switch methods: Ensure appropriate timing based on menstrual cycle.

Replacement rules depend on age timing of last menstrual period.

Legal advice should be sought if there is any doubt as to whether a person has the mental capacity to consent to a procedure that will permanently remove their fertility.
Written consent should be obtained from individuals wishing to undergo vasectomy or laparoscopic or hysteroscopic tubal occlusion.
All verbal advice must be supported by accurate, impartial, printed or recorded information.
Advice post-vasectomy: Men who have undergone vasectomy should be provided with a post- procedural information leaflet that outlines appropriate self-care and instructions.
Advice post-tubal occlusion: Women should be provided with information about the method of tubal occlusion undertaken and: of any complications.
Additional contraception: Individuals who have undergone vasectomy should be informed of the need to use additional contraception until sterility is confirmed.

Regret: Additional care must be taken when counselling individuals under the age of 30 years or individuals without children who request sterilization. If tubal occlusion is performed at the same time as a caesarean section, counselling and agreement should be given at least 2 weeks in advance of the procedure.
LA is ➡️ infiltration of the subcuticular tissue ➡️ direct injection to the vas deferens.

Cauterization followed by division of the vas deferens, with or without excision, is associated with the lowest likelihood of early recanalization (failure) when compared to other occlusion techniques.
Clips are not recommended for occluding the vas deferens as their use is associated with a potentially high failure rate when compared to other occlusion methods.
Post-vasectomy semen analysis (PVSA) should be carried out to identify early failure.
If motile sperm are observed in a fresh sample 7 months post-procedure, the vasectomy should be considered a failure.
Bleeding: Health professionals should cauterize or suture any bleeding peri vasal and subdermal blood vessels to ensure haemostasis.
Pain: Health professionals should consider the administration of additional Anaesthesia/analgesia.
Infection: The routine use of prophylactic antibiotics is not recommended prior to vasectomy.
Early failure: Clinicians should modify their technique if overall failure attributable to technical failure, recanalization and non-compliance with additional contraception is more than 1%.
The contraceptive failure rate should be quoted as approximately 1 in 2000 (0.05%).

Interventions for chronic post-vasectomy pain: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and treatment to alleviate neuropathic pain are common first-line treatment options for chronic post-vasectomy pain (CPVP).

Prostate and testicular cancer: There is no evidence of an increase in testicular cancers associated with vasectomy. The weak association observed in some studies between vasectomy and prostatic cancer is unlikely to be causal.
Reversal: Vasectomy reversal involves complex surgery that can result in high postoperative patency rates, but may not result in pregnancy or a return to fertility.
Culdoscopy should not be used as a method of approach for sterilization.
The laparoscopic approach to the fallopian tubes is quicker to perform and results in less minor morbidity compared to mini-laparotomy.

All women should be informed of the risks associated with laparoscopy and when this may proceed to laparotomy. In some cases, laparoscopy/laparotomy may be contraindicated and consideration should be given to other methods.
Any effective surgical or mechanical method of tubal occlusion can be used when mini laparotomy the method of approach for an interval sterilization.
For postpartum sterilization, both Filshie clips and modified Pomeroy technique are effective. Filshie clip application is quicker to perform.
of the fallopian tubes by Filshie clips should be the method of choice for laparoscopic tubal occlusion.

A pregnancy test must be performed before sterilization to exclude the possibility of a preexisting pregnancy. However, a negative test result does not exclude the possibility of a luteal phase pregnancy.

Tubal occlusion can be performed at any time during the menstrual cycle, providing that the woman has a negative pregnancy test and is not at risk of luteal-phase pregnancy [unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI) in the past 3 weeks]. If this is not the case, the procedure should be deferred and contraception used until at least 3 weeks from the last instance of UPSI.
Stopping contraception after laparoscopic tubal occlusion:
CHC, the POP or non-hormonal contraception should be advised to continue their contraceptive method for at least 7 days after laparoscopic sterilization.

If the progestogen only injectable or implant is being used, laparoscopic tubal occlusion can be carried out at any time during the period of licensed use without the need for additional contraception.
The progestogen-only implant can be removed at the time of the procedure or any time following laparoscopic tubal occlusion.
If a Cu-lUD or LNG-IUS is in situ prior to sterilization, this should be retained and removed at least 1 week after dafter laparoscopic tubal occlusion.

Following sterilization via hysteroscopy and the insertion of intra-fallopian micro-inserts, additional contraception must be used until either successful insert placement and/or tubal occlusion are confirmed.
Intraoperative complications with tubal micro-inserts: a low level of intraoperative complications in a minority of patients.
Postoperative complications of hysteroscopic sterilization: with a low level of postoperative complications.

A confirmatory imaging test should be undertaken 3 months after the insertion of intra-fallopian micro-inserts. This may be via X-ray or transvaginal hysterosalpingogram (HSG) in selected patients where X-ray/TVUSS cannot confirm satisfactory placement.

In the UK and Europe, the placement of an Essure® device can be followed up by performing a pelvic ultrasound scan at 3 months post-procedure.

In the USA, it was mandatory until recently to perform HSG (hysterosalpingogram) to confirm device position and tubal occlusion 3 months after the procedure. In difficult cases or where the device is not easily visualized, a modified HSG technique is used, in which contrast media is instilled gently to allow cornual filling.

Four radiographic markers are used as landmarks to confirm satisfactory location and tubal occlusion. Satisfactory location is defined as having less than 50% of the inner coil trailing into the uterine cavity or when the proximal marker of the inner coil is 30 mm or closer from where the contrast fills the uterine cornua.
The FDA approved transvaginal ultrasound in as a confirmation test to confirm tubal occlusion in the USA.

The Essure® device is magnetic resonance-conditional, meaning a woman with an Essure® device can undergo MRI scanning with static magnetic field of 3 tesla or less and maximum spatial gradient of magnetic field of 720 gauss/cm or less.
Ovarian cancer: protective effect against developing ovarian cancer that persists over time

content_blocks.content: Quick starting is the term used to describe immediate initiation of a contraceptive method at the time a woman requests it rather than waiting for the start of the next natural menstrual period.

Healthcare practitioners (HCPs) can offer quick start of any method of contraception at any time in the menstrual cycle if it is reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant or at risk of pregnancy from recent unprotected sexual intercourse (UPSI).
Quick Starting if Pregnancy Cannot Be Excluded
Women who have a negative HSUP but are at risk of pregnancy from recent UPSI should be advised that:
Pregnancy cannot be excluded by an HSUP until >21 days after the last UPSI.
EC may be indicated. CHC, POP and IMP can be quick started if they prefer not to delay starting contraception.
DMPA may be considered if other methods are not suitable or acceptable.
LNG-IUS should not generally be quick started unless pregnancy can be reasonably excluded.
(Note: HSUP = highly sensitive urinary pregnancy test, able to detect hCG levels around 20 mIU/ml)
CHC containing cyproterone acetate should not be quick started unless pregnancy can be reasonably excluded.
A Cu-IUD can be quick started only if the indications for use as EC are met. After LNG-EC administration, CHC, POP, IMP (and DMPA) can be quick started immediately.
After UPA-EC administration, they should wait 5 days before quick starting suitable hormonal contraception [CHC, POP, IMP (and DMPA)].
Additional contraceptive precautions (barrier or abstinence) are required until the quick started contraceptive method becomes effective.
A follow-up HSUP is required no sooner than 21 days after the last UPSI.

Important consideration before providing contraction to young people:

Young people under 18 years to 25 years:Whilst the age of consent to sexual activity in the UK is 16 years, surveys suggest that approximately one in three young people have had sexual intercourse by this age.
Confidentiality:Young people should always be made aware of confidentiality policies, including situations where confidentiality may need to be breached.
Safeguarding young people:All sexual and reproductive health care services should have a named person identified as the local lead for child protection.

Perform the suction as is done during a first trimester aspiration abortion, rotating the cannula during suction. If using MVA empty the aspirator when it is full and repeat as necessary. When nothing more can be suctioned, remove cannula from uterus.

Maintaining gentle traction on the tenacullum to straighten the cervical canal, pass the closed foreceps through the cervix in a vertical direction (the jaw of the bierer or Sopher forceps should open in an up-down direction, not horizontally). See fig 2.

As soon as the forceps pass through the internal os, gently open it as wide as possible. While opening the forceps, drop your hand and forceps in the direction of the floor to angle the jaws of the forceps into the anterior lower – uterine segment (see Figure 3).
A mid trimester gravid uterus is usually positioned anteriorly, toward the anterior abdominal wall.
To evacuate the tissue, close the forceps around the fetal tissue and rotated it 90 degrees to assist with disarticulation before withdrawing.
Be careful not to grasp the myometrium with the forceps.
Keep forceps within the lower to mid – uterine segment. There is usually no need to use the forceps near the fundus, which increases the risk of perforation (see Figure 4).

attempt to remove tissues with each pass of the forceps.
If you cannot locate and move the fetus/ fetal parts within 5 – 7 minutes, consider using ultrasound to visualize and direct the movement of the forceps.

If the tissue has moved upwards to the fundus from the lower segment of the uterus, use suction to bring the fetus down within grasp of the forceps or consider removing the speculum and tenacullum and messaging the uterus. If dilated sufficiently to allow passage of part of the provider’s hand, the pregnancy can be repositioned internally. In the unlikely event that these maneuvers do not bring the tissue within reach of the forceps, administer misoprostal 400mcg (buccal) or high dose oxytocin (200 units in 500mL normal saline or lactated ringers and run at 50Ml/hour IV). The D&E procedure should be reattempted in 30 minutes to 3 hours, the woman should be observed during this time.
When all the fetal tissues is removed, perform suction aspiration to ensure no tissues are remaining.

Identify fetal parts (Thorax, spine, calvarium, all 4 extremities and placenta, for all procedures, 14 weeks’ and greater).

content_blocks.content: The patient is placed in the dorsal lithotomy position. The pelvis and large intestine are prepared for surgery.
A bimanual examination under general anesthesia is performed to differentiate between an enterocele and a rectocele.
Observation of the perineal body is made to determine the extent of reconstruction needed

The labia are retracted with interrupted sutures. The upper extent of the rectocele is identified. Allis clamps are applied to the posterior vaginal mucosa over this area. The clamps are elevated, creating a triangle.

Allis clamps are placed at the margins of the original hymen. An additional Allis clamp is placed in the midline at the top of the rectocele. A transverse incision is made at the posterior fourchette.A Kelly clamp is inserted under the posterior vaginal mucosa, dissecting the posterior mucosa off the perirectal fascia. An additional incision is made in the perineal body, removing a triangular piece of skin, outlined by the dotted line. This will expose the insertion of the bulbocavernosus muscle. Only the skin of the perineal body should be removed, and care should be taken not to remove the underlying superficial transverse perineal muscles.

The vertical incision in the posterior vaginal mucosa has been made, and the edges are held with Allis clamps. The perirectal fascia is dissected off the posterior vaginal mucosa. The apex of the rectocele is held in an Allis clamp. The dissection of perirectal fascia off the vaginal mucosa is started with a scalpel but is completed with the handle of the scalpel or with scissors.

A finger is placed over the rectocele, pushing it into the rectum, thus revealing the margins of the levator ani muscles. Already, number 1synthetic absorbable suture is passed through the margin of the levator ani from the apex down to the posterior fourchette. Bydepressing the anterior rectal wall downward with one finger and elevating the previously placed suture, the surgeon sees the margin of the levator ani more clearly, and placement of sutures becomes easier.
After all levator ani sutures have been placed, they are progressively tied.

The excessive posterior vaginal mucosa has been trimmed away; the triangular defect in the perineal body can be seen. The insertion of the bulbocavernosus muscle is adjacent to the triangular defect in the perineal body.
The perirectal fascia is closed with interrupted 0 synthetic absorbable suture in the midline

A synthetic absorbable suture is placed at the apex of the vaginal mucosa and tied (a).The tail of the suture is left for a length of 20 cm.The suture (b) is placed superficial to the tail of the suture (a).

The closure of the posterior vaginal wall is completed to the posterior fourchette. The former hymenal ring is reconstructed. The suture (b) is tied to the tail of the first suture (a) placed at the apex. The vaginal mucosa is approximated to the perirectal fascia to eliminate dead space

The same suture completes the closure of the perineal body. Several interrupted O synthetic absorbable sutures are placed in the insertions of the bulbocavernosus muscles to reconstruct the perineal body.
The posterior vaginal mucosa suture (b) is placed in the subcutaneous tissue of the perineal body. Note that the suture marked a is still left long for eventual tying.
The same suture (b) that completed the closure of the posterior vaginal wall is used to close the
subcutaneous tissue and the insertions of the bulbocavernosus muscles.
The suture marked a is the long end of the tie at the apex of the posterior vaginal mucosa incision

The subcuticular suture (b) is placed in the skin of the perineal body from the apex of the wound immediately above the anus to the posterior fourchette. At the posterior fourchette it is tied to suture a.
The completed operation is shown, with the rectocele reduced and the perineal body reconstructed. Vaginal packs are not required. Bladder catheterization is rarely indicated.

topics.title: 6.2.PERINATAL MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 6.2.PERINATAL MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: Specialist perinatal mental health services (PMHS) are concerned with the prevention, detection and management of mental health problems that can complicate pregnancy and the postnatal period.

This includes offering pre-conception counselling, caring for women with new-onset or pre-existing moderate to severe mental illness, as well as caring for women with a history of illness who are currently well but who are at high risk of serious mental illness during the perinatal period.

Promoting the emotional and physical well-being and healthy development of babies and infants, through supporting a secure and attuned relationship with their parents, is central to the care provided by a specialist PMHS.
Specialist perinatal mental health services include specialist community perinatal mental health teams and MBUs.

Specialist community perinatal mental health teams have the dual role of assessing and treating severe and moderate mental illness with additional complex psychosocial needs or comorbid conditions, as well as assessing and actively supporting the mother-infant relationship.

Women who need admission in late pregnancy or the postpartum period should be admitted to specialist mother and baby units which are designed and resourced to safely meet the physical and mental health needs of both mother and infant.
Each specialist perinatal mental health service should be part of a managed clinical network.
Perinatal mental health problems include a range of disorders and severities, which present in a variety of health settings and are managed by multiple services.
Some of these services are specifically designed to meet the needs of pregnant and postpartum women and their infants, others care for them as part of a general service.

content_blocks.content: Clinical Governance is defined as a framework through which NHS organizations are accountable for continuously improving the quality of the services and safeguarding standards of the care by creating an environment in which excellence in the clinical care will flourish.
Traditionally, clinical governance has been described using 7 key pillars:
The various elements of clinical governance, when brought together, acquire the ability to improve the efficiency of systems

topics.title: 2. CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS
topics.description: Detailed medical reference and study guide on 2. CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS.
topics.author: Dr. Farzana Muneer

content_blocks.content: means ensuring that everything you do is designed to provide the best outcomes for patients ensuring that the right person does:
In the right way (skills and competence)
At the right time (providing treatment/services when the patient needs them)
In the right place (location of treatment/services)
With the right result (clinical effectiveness/maximizing health gain).
The best available evidence, clinical skills and patient preferences are combined to achieve optimal processes and outcomes.
Adopting an evidence-based approach in the management of patient (evidence from randomized controlled trials, meta-analysis and systematic reviews)
Changing practice, developing new protocols or guidelines based on experience and evidence if current practice is inadequate

Implementing NICE guidelines, National Service Frameworks and other national standards to ensure optimal care - these should be appropriately disseminated and implemented in clinical practice, and compliance can be monitored by means of clinical audit
Clinical audit can be seen as a tool for driving clinical effectiveness.
But clinical effectiveness also needs to encompass broader, qualitative aspects of care:
sensitivity to the personal needs of the patient.

Understanding these aspects of patient care forces us to recognize the diversity of patients. Not just in terms of gender, ethnicity or sexuality but also capacity, social background and acknowledging previous experiences. This enables us to personalize care and integrate clinical effectiveness with patients' previous experiences. This is the basis of person-center care ('what matters to you' rather than 'what’s the matter with you'). Clinical governance therefore needs to foster and promote this side of care as integral to the improvement of services and is likely to achieve better outcomes.  Ultimately therapies are only of value if patients accept and believe in them. Finding the right prompts is the key to reaching an agreement with patients and is most likely to result in successful therapies.

The aim of audit is to ensure clinical practice is continuously monitored and that deficiencies in relation to set standards of care are remedied.

Criterion-based clinical audits assess local clinical performance against agreed standards, implement changes to clinical practice in order to enhance performance, and then reassess performance. This is a cyclical quality improvement process. Clinical audit usually assesses one or more of the following domains:
Audit can be considered to have five principal steps, commonly referred to as the audit cycle
3. Data collection to assess performance against the prespecified standard

Responsibilities for filling the maternity dashboard.

The primary objective is maternity dashboard is to ensure continuous improvement in the clinical care with clearly defined mechanisms and named individual responsible identified to deal with these issues as they arise.

The score card also provides information to establish trends such as increase in the number of caesarean sections requires an input from obstetrician, labour ward, clinical lead, third and the fourth degree, perineal tears, patient complaints.

Since it is important for someone with a clinical risk perspective to be responsible for maternity dashboard, such a person could be the risk manager, lead midwife for the risk working closely with the lead consultant for the labour ward. It is also shared with consumer representative in the Labor Board Forum and maternity Services liaison committees.
Advantages and the disadvantages of Maternity Dashboard.
It improved the overall quality of care by informing the health providers about the performance
to stimulate the comparisons between other maternity units to identify the areas for the further improvement.
It helped to understand how processes for delivering the health care services are designed to meet patient quality and operational requirements, including the best practice requirements.
Helped to design and deliver the processes are coordinated and tested to ensure the smooth delivery of maternity care.
The only disadvantage is that we consider it as another paper exercise. To avoid this pitfall, it is important to modify the Maternity Dashboard to suit local needs.
